units.translation: greaves, a spear, and defenses of rocks

it is also written 'of wings', and you might say 'of rocks' thus: the defenses of rocks, that is, the shield, which we hold before our body and by which we receive the stones coming at us from our enemies; but if 'of wings', understand 'defenses' as arrows
I inquire, a poetic present form for the common πυνθάνομαι [I inquire], from which the remaining tenses are taken.
I inquire whether Menelaus will return home safe and sound with you.
I learn from my eyes the return.
But now, wretched, I learn that he is dead.
I learn that some are saying a new report.
that he himself should inquire about their husband.
Thus Scaliger for πειθοῖ [persuasion]. It is not found in other writers.
She brings us some new tidings, friends.
By tidings of what message are you sent to sacrifice?
of a torch cut from a pine
The proper meaning is 'of pine, pitchy'.
Oppian seems to have used it in the sense of 'bitter'.
which the scholiast explains by πικρά [bitter].

where, since the meter requires the first syllable to be short, I have restored πυκάεντ᾽ [dense, thick], comparing Theognostus Can. p. 23, 12, who explains πυκᾶες [dense, thick] by ἰσχυρόν [strong], where he discusses words beginning with πυ [py]. But lest anyone attribute the strange ending of the word to a scribal error, another passage of the same grammarian prevents it, p. 131, 29: τὰ εἰς ἐς οὐδέτερα οἷον τὸ Κυνόσαργες προπαροξύτονον, καὶ τὸ πεύκαες, ῥώπαες, δονάκαες [neuter nouns ending in -ες, such as Κυνόσαργες [Cynosarges] with antepenultimate accent, and πεύκαες [pine-like], ῥώπαες [brush-like], δονάκαες [reed-like]], where πεύκαες [pine-like] (which should be written πύκαες [dense, thick]) and δονάκαες [reed-like] are nothing other than what the scholiast on Homer Il. 18, 576 (on the words παρὰ ῥοδανὸν δονακῆα [along the waving reed-bed]) mentioned: φησὶ δὲ Διονύσιος γράφεσθαι καὶ δονακῆεν κατὰ τὸ οὐδέτερον, ὡς καὶ τὸν πευκῶνα πευκᾶεν [Dionysius says that it is also written δονακῆεν [reedy] in the neuter, just as the pine-grove is called πευκᾶεν [piney]]. As for the meaning, since it is not established that πύκη [dense] was said for πεύκη [pine], perhaps it should be derived from πύκα [densely], so that it is the same as πυκνόν [dense]: to which Theognostus' interpretation ἰσχυρόν [strong] better suits than an adjective derived from πεύκη [pine], and perhaps the scholiast meant the same, who interpreted it more freely as πανηγυρικόν, λαμπρόν [festive, splendid].
and they armed themselves with sharp stings among the fish, the goby, etc.
may it be mine to raise a piercing cry of triumph over a man being slain and a woman perishing
